title: Raising concerns & whistleblowing
blurb: GDC Principle 8, what counts as a concern, who to go to inside and outside the practice, and how the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 protects you.
question: You notice the autoclave log has been filled in for days when the machine wasn't run, and a colleague tells you to 'just sign it, everyone does'. You're worried about patient safety but also about your job. What should you do, who should you tell, and what protects you?

teach.h: Patients first, even when it's awkward
teach.body: GDC Principle 8 says you must raise concerns if patients are at risk. This duty overrides any personal or professional loyalty to colleagues or your employer. You don't need proof: if you have a genuine, reasonable concern, raise it, even if you are not certain. Raise it promptly, because delay can leave patients at risk. Investigating is someone else's job; your job is to speak up.

rows.label: Instruments not properly decontaminated, or logs falsified
A colleague seems impaired by alcohol, drugs or ill health
A colleague's treatment or behaviour is unsafe
Being asked to work beyond your training or scope
Signs that a child or adult is being abused

teach.note: Safeguarding concerns follow the practice's safeguarding procedure and the local authority route. See the safeguarding lessons.

steps.label: GDC
steps.sub: If a registrant's fitness to practise is in question

teach.caption: Start inside the practice where you can. If the concern is about the person you would normally go to, or you fear a cover-up, you can go straight to an outside body.

teach.body: If you're told your concern has been 'noted' but nothing changes, take it to the next level of the agreed procedure. Keep a brief, factual record of what you raised, when and with whom. You can get confidential advice from your indemnity provider, a trade union or the whistleblowing charity Protect. If you are asked to follow an instruction you believe is unsafe, raise your concern before acting, not afterwards.

head: Question
In brief
rows: Workers, including employees and agency staff
Disclosures you reasonably believe are in the public interest
Danger to health or safety, crime, cover-ups
Your employer or a prescribed body, e.g. GDC, CQC
teach.caption: This is 'whistleblowing'. PIDA amended the Employment Rights Act 1996. Agreements that try to stop you making a protected disclosure ('gagging clauses') cannot remove this protection.

teach.body: A comment like 'just sign the log, everyone does' points to a cultural problem: unsafe shortcuts have become normal. That itself is a concern to raise. Every practice should have a raising concerns (whistleblowing) policy and a named person, and GDC standards say anyone who employs or manages staff must encourage an open culture where concerns can be raised without fear. As a nurse, you also support colleagues who speak up.

teach.h: Asked to do something you think is unsafe?

root.label: Unsafe instruction
root.sub: Raise it there and then, before acting

teach.text: You do NOT need proof or certainty before raising a concern. Waiting until you are 100% sure can leave patients at risk. A reasonable belief is enough, and PIDA protects you even if the concern later turns out to be mistaken, provided your belief was reasonable.

items: GDC Principle 8: raise concerns if patients are at risk, even if you are not certain.
The duty overrides loyalty to colleagues or employer.
Go to the named person or manager first; escalate if nothing changes or if internal routes aren't safe.
Outside bodies include the NHS commissioner, CQC and GDC.
PIDA 1998 protects workers who make public interest disclosures from dismissal and detriment.

summary: You can now recognise when something is a concern rather than a grievance, raise it promptly without needing proof, follow the route from the named person through to outside bodies such as the CQC and GDC, escalate when nothing changes, and explain how PIDA 1998 protects whistleblowers.

A.q: A dental nurse believes a colleague's practice is putting patients at risk but isn't completely sure. What does the GDC expect?
options: Gather proof before saying anything
Raise the concern even without certainty
Wait to see if a patient complains first
Discuss it with friends outside work
A.why: The GDC expects you to raise a genuine concern promptly, even if you are not certain. Investigation is for others.

whyNot.0: Waiting for proof delays action and can leave patients at risk.
whyNot.2: Patients shouldn't have to be harmed or complain before a concern is raised.
whyNot.3: Discussing it outside work breaches confidentiality and doesn't protect patients.

A.q: A nurse raises a concern and is told it has been 'noted', but nothing changes. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Drop it, since it has now been formally noted
Post about it on social media to warn people
Escalate it through the agreed procedure
Resign quietly and say nothing further about it
A.why: If a concern isn't acted on, you escalate it to the next level of the practice's procedure or to an outside body.

whyNot.0: Patients remain at risk if nothing changes, so the duty to act continues.
whyNot.1: Social media is inappropriate, breaches confidentiality and is not a protected route.
whyNot.3: Leaving doesn't remove the risk to patients or your duty to raise it.

A.q: A nurse wants to raise a concern but fears it will cost her job. What protection exists?
options: None; it is a personal risk she must take
Only if she is a union member
Only once the concern is proven true
Law protects public interest disclosures
A.why: The Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 protects workers from dismissal or detriment for raising concerns in the public interest.

whyNot.0: Workers are protected by law when they make protected disclosures.
whyNot.1: PIDA protection doesn't depend on union membership.
whyNot.2: A reasonable belief is enough; the concern doesn't have to be proven.

B.q: A nurse is told by a colleague to 'just sign the sterilisation log, everyone does'. What does this most likely indicate?
options: A cultural problem that should be raised
A normal shortcut that is fine on busy days
A personal grievance with the colleague
An admin issue for reception to handle
B.why: Falsifying logs being treated as normal suggests an unsafe culture, which is a patient-safety concern to raise.

whyNot.1: Signing for checks that weren't done is never acceptable, however busy the day.
whyNot.2: This is about patient safety, not a personal employment issue.
whyNot.3: Decontamination records are a clinical safety matter, not a reception task.

B.q: A nurse is unsure who to raise a clinical concern with. What should the practice have in place?
options: A suggestion box in the staff room
A named person and a clear route
An annual meeting for complaints
A rule that only dentists raise concerns
B.why: Practices should have a raising concerns policy with a named contact and a clear route, so anyone can speak up.

whyNot.0: An anonymous box may help but doesn't provide a clear, accountable route.
whyNot.2: Waiting for an annual meeting delays action on patient safety.
whyNot.3: Every registrant, including dental nurses, has the duty to raise concerns.

B.q: Which of these is a grievance rather than a patient-safety concern?
options: A colleague smelling of alcohol at work
Instruments reused without sterilising
Disagreeing with your holiday allocation
Being asked to take X-rays without training
B.why: A disagreement about your own holiday is a personal employment matter for the grievance procedure.

whyNot.0: A possibly impaired colleague is a risk to patients and a concern to raise.
whyNot.1: Inadequate decontamination is a clear risk to patients.
whyNot.3: Working beyond your training puts patients at risk and is a concern.

C.q: The dentist asks you to do something you believe is unsafe. What should you do?
options: Raise it first; escalate if unresolved
Do it, since the dentist is responsible
Do it, then report it to the manager afterwards
Refuse and leave the surgery at once
C.why: You should raise your concern before carrying out an instruction you think is unsafe, and escalate if it isn't resolved.

whyNot.1: You are accountable for your own actions, even when following instructions.
whyNot.2: Reporting afterwards means the patient may already have been harmed.
whyNot.3: Walking out abandons the patient; raise the concern calmly first.

C.q: Your concern is about the practice owner, so you can't raise it internally. Which body could you go to?
options: A local newspaper
The patient's family
The practice's own accountant
The Care Quality Commission
C.why: The CQC is a prescribed body for disclosures about health and social care services, so going to it is protected.

whyNot.0: Going to the media is rarely protected unless strict conditions are met; prescribed bodies come first.
whyNot.1: Telling a patient's family breaches confidentiality and isn't a proper route.
whyNot.2: An accountant has no role in investigating patient-safety concerns.

C.q: Which statement about the duty to raise concerns is correct?
options: It applies only to dentists and therapists
It overrides loyalty to colleagues
It needs written proof first
It applies only to NHS practices
C.why: GDC guidance is clear that protecting patients comes before personal or professional loyalties.

whyNot.0: Every GDC registrant, including dental nurses, has this duty.
whyNot.2: A reasonable concern is enough; proof isn't required.
whyNot.3: The duty applies in every setting, NHS and private.

reteach.title: Pull the cord
reteach.question: On a train, any passenger can pull the emergency cord if they see danger, without needing to be the driver or to be certain. How is raising a concern similar?

blocks.body: You don't have to be the most senior person, and you don't have to be sure. If you see something that could hurt patients, you pull the cord: tell the named person or your manager. If they don't respond, you go to the next carriage (the practice owner), then to the guard outside (the NHS commissioner, CQC or GDC). The law (PIDA 1998) makes sure you can't be punished for pulling the cord when you reasonably believe the public is at risk.

explain.body: Principle 8: raise concerns if patients are at risk. Act promptly, don't wait for proof, and put patients before loyalty to colleagues or employer.

items.label: GDC Principle: raise concerns if patients are at risk
proof needed: a reasonable concern is enough

test.q: Which GDC principle covers raising concerns?
options: Principle 2
Principle 5
Principle 8
Principle 9
test.why: GDC Principle 8 is 'Raise concerns if patients are at risk'.

whyNot.0: Principle 2 is about communicating effectively with patients.
whyNot.1: Principle 5 is about having a clear and effective complaints procedure.
whyNot.3: Principle 9 is about personal behaviour maintaining confidence in the profession.

explain.body: Start with the named person or line manager, then the practice owner. If that fails or isn't appropriate, go to an outside body such as the NHS commissioner or CQC, or the GDC for fitness to practise concerns.

test.q: Where should a nurse usually raise a patient-safety concern first?
options: With the GDC directly, by phone
With the named lead or manager
With the patient involved
On the staff messaging group chat
test.why: The usual first step is the practice's named person or line manager, unless that isn't appropriate.

whyNot.0: The GDC is for fitness to practise concerns, usually after internal routes or where they aren't suitable.
whyNot.2: Patients aren't the route for raising internal safety concerns.
whyNot.3: Group chats aren't a formal or confidential route.

explain.body: Workers who make a disclosure they reasonably believe is in the public interest, to their employer or a prescribed body such as the GDC or CQC, are protected from dismissal and detriment.

test.q: What does the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 do?
options: Requires patients to report poor care
Sets time limits for complaints
Lets employers silence staff legally
Protects workers who blow the whistle
test.why: PIDA protects workers from dismissal or detriment when they make protected disclosures in the public interest.

whyNot.0: PIDA is about workers, not a duty on patients.
whyNot.1: Complaint time limits come from complaints procedures, not PIDA.
whyNot.2: PIDA does the opposite: gagging clauses can't stop protected disclosures.
